metadata.title: How Load Balancers Handle Millions of Requests
metadata.audience: backend engineers, software engineers, technical learners
metadata.creator: Akshay Chavan
metadata.note: 4K UHD landscape master. Clean load-balancer diagrams with protected title, diagram, and caption zones.

skin_warnings: B00: palette=claude but the cold open is 'un-annotated' — COLD OPEN LAW wants ClaudeComposerAsk

beats.role_note: Cold open: establish the scale of incoming application traffic.
beats.narration_text: Every second, popular applications can receive millions of requests.

visual.title: MILLIONS OF REQUESTS
visual.concept: A large stream of compact request markers flows from users toward an application.
visual.layout: Keep title in the upper safe zone. Request markers occupy the center. Keep the lower caption zone clear.
visual.safety: No arrows or request markers may overlap the title or caption.

beats.role_note: Show why one backend server becomes a bottleneck.
beats.narration_text: Send all that traffic to one server, and it quickly becomes overwhelmed.

visual.title: ONE SERVER. TOO MUCH TRAFFIC.
visual.concept: Many requests converge on a single backend server which becomes overloaded.
visual.layout: Requests remain on the left and server on the right with a dedicated horizontal traffic lane between them.
visual.safety: Arrows must stop at the outer edge of the server box. Never draw connectors through text or through the server.

beats.role_note: Introduce horizontal scaling and the routing problem it creates.
beats.narration_text: Adding more servers helps, but now something has to decide where each request goes.

visual.title: MORE SERVERS. NOW WHAT?
visual.concept: Three backend servers appear while incoming requests wait for a routing decision.
visual.layout: Requests occupy the left zone. S1, S2, and S3 are vertically separated in the right zone. Keep the middle routing zone empty.
visual.safety: Do not connect requests directly to every server yet. Maintain clear spacing between all server boxes.

beats.role_note: Introduce the load balancer and its position in the architecture.
beats.narration_text: That's the job of a load balancer. It sits between users and your servers.

visual.title: THE LOAD BALANCER
visual.concept: Users send traffic to one load balancer, which distributes it across three backend servers.
visual.layout: Three fixed columns: USERS on left, LOAD BALANCER in center, SERVERS on right. Servers are vertically separated.
visual.safety: All arrows connect edge-to-edge. User arrows end at the left edge of the load balancer. Backend arrows start at its right edge and terminate at server edges. No arrow passes through a box or label.

beats.narration_text: A simple strategy like round robin sends each new request to the next server.

visual.title: ROUND ROBIN
visual.concept: Sequential requests are routed in order to S1, S2, S3, then back to S1.
visual.layout: Load balancer remains left-of-center and three servers remain vertically stacked on the right. Animate one route at a time.
visual.safety: Do not display all moving arrows on top of one another. Use distinct routes or sequential animation so connectors remain readable.

beats.role_note: Explain least-connections routing as an alternative.
beats.narration_text: Other strategies can route traffic to the server handling the fewest active connections.

visual.title: LEAST CONNECTIONS
visual.concept: Each server displays a small active-connection count. The next request is routed to the least busy server.
visual.layout: Connection counters sit beside, not inside, the traffic paths. Highlight only the selected server and route.
visual.safety: Counters must not overlap server labels. The selected request arrow must terminate at the selected server edge.

beats.role_note: Show health checks detecting an unavailable backend.
beats.narration_text: Load balancers also perform health checks to find servers that stop responding.

visual.title: HEALTH CHECKS
visual.concept: The load balancer checks S1, S2, and S3. S2 stops responding and is marked unavailable.
visual.layout: Keep health-check indicators in a separate lane from user traffic. S2 receives a clear unavailable indicator.
visual.safety: Health-check arrows must not cross server names or traffic arrows. Keep failure annotation adjacent to S2 rather than over the box.

beats.role_note: Demonstrate traffic being routed around a failed server.
beats.narration_text: Traffic is then sent only to healthy servers, keeping the application available.

visual.title: ROUTE AROUND FAILURE
visual.concept: S2 remains unavailable while new requests are distributed between healthy S1 and S3.
visual.layout: S1 and S3 retain active traffic lanes. S2 stays visible but visually inactive.
visual.safety: No request arrow should point toward S2. Routes to S1 and S3 must be spatially separated and edge-to-edge.

beats.narration_text: That's how load balancing turns a pool of servers into one scalable, resilient service.

visual.title: SCALE WITHOUT A SINGLE SERVER BOTTLENECK
visual.concept: Final clean architecture: users flow through the load balancer to a healthy pool of backend servers.
visual.layout: Use a centered, symmetrical architecture with generous spacing and minimal annotation.
visual.safety: Keep the final frame uncluttered. No crossing connectors, no overlapping labels, and no objects outside the 16:9 safe area.

beats.narration_text: For more explainers on the systems behind modern software, follow Humanitarians AI.
